708.title: Blandina of Lyon (177)
708.hook: an enslaved woman outlasts her torturers with one short answer
708.howItsDone: Catholics remember the martyrs of Lyon, Saint Pothinus the bishop, Saint Blandina and their companions, together in the Church's calendar of saints, and their story is read from the letter Eusebius preserved.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Justin the apologist, and the Sunday he described to the emperor. Your line was the same Mass.

Her owner was afraid for her. That's where her part of the story begins. Persecution has broken out in Lyon, a city in Gaul, and Christians are being dragged before the crowd. Among them are Blandina, who is enslaved, and the woman who owns her. The other Christians are afraid for her too. Her body seems weak, and they fear she won't even manage to say what she believes. The letter that tells this story was written by the Christians of Lyon and Vienne, and it has a surprise in it. The one they worried about becomes the one the letter dwells on.
screen: `HER OWNER WAS AFRAID FOR HER.` → `LYON, IN GAUL.` → `THE ONE THEY WORRIED ABOUT.`

segments.voice: Eusebius, the Church historian, copied the letter into his history, so it can still be read. First, the doubt. Blandina's own people expect her to break. She's enslaved, and she's frail. Second, the torturers give up. The letter says they took turns on her from morning until evening, until they were worn out themselves. They admitted they were beaten. They had nothing more to do to her, and were amazed she was still breathing. Third, her answer. The charge hanging over the Christians is the old slander that they do terrible things in secret, the same rumors Justin was answering yesterday. Her answer, in Greek: Christianē eimi. Christian, I am. And among us, nothing evil is done. The letter says saying it gave her strength again, and rest, and took away the pain. The answer wasn't a speech. It was a name, and she held to it. Fourth, the stake. Later she's hung on a stake in the arena, and the letter says the others, looking at her stretched out there, saw in their sister the one who was crucified for them. An enslaved woman became the picture of Christ for those suffering with her. The Church still remembers the martyrs of Lyon together, and Blandina's name stands beside her bishop's. It's a story about courage, and also about who gets underestimated. The one nobody expected to stand turned out to be holding everyone else up.
screen: `THEY EXPECTED HER TO BREAK.` · `THE TORTURERS GAVE UP.` · `THE SAME ANSWER, OVER AND OVER.` · `THEY SAW CHRIST IN HER.` · then, large: `CHRISTIAN, I AM.`

segments.voice: Blandina's answer was short, and she held to it. Look for one small thing in your life that bends too easily, an honest answer you tend to blur, a promise you keep postponing, and picture yourself holding steady, without a speech, just the same quiet answer. If you pray, ask God for a little of her steadiness.
Christianē eimi. Greek for Christian, I am: Blandina's short answer, repeated until it gave her strength again. Today's word.
Your line: Christian, I am. Blandina's Greek, said until it gave her strength. Day seven hundred eight.

709.title: Irenaeus (c. 180)
709.hook: the glory of God is a human being fully alive
709.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Irenaeus as a bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his line on the glory of God is quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church in its teaching on creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Blandina of Lyon, whose short answer, Christianē eimi, outlasted her torturers. Your line was Christian, I am.

An old friend has drifted into strange teachings, and a bishop writes to call him back. To make his point, he reaches for a memory. When I was a boy, he says, I heard Polycarp. I can still tell you the place where he sat to teach, how he came and went, how he talked about John and the others who had seen the Lord. The bishop is Irenaeus, and Eusebius kept the letter. After the martyrs of Lyon, the church there needs a new bishop. It gets this man, who carries Polycarp's voice in his head.
screen: `A LETTER TO AN OLD FRIEND.` → `I HEARD POLYCARP.` → `A NEW BISHOP FOR LYON.`

segments.voice: Irenaeus wrote a long work that came to be called Against Heresies. First, what he was up against. Some teachers of his day said the material world was a mistake, made by a lesser power. The body was a cage. Salvation was secret knowledge, handed to a few who were in on it. Second, his answer. One God, he says, made heaven and earth, and made them good. The same God formed the human being from the earth, and the Son of God took real flesh. So the body isn't a prison to escape. It's part of what God is saving. Third, the line. In the Latin text it begins: Gloria enim Dei vivens homo. For the glory of God is a living human being. The Catechism of the Catholic Church gives it this way: the glory of God is man fully alive. That's today's line. Fourth, the second half. The sentence keeps going: and the life of a human being is the vision of God. Fully alive, for Irenaeus, isn't the same as busy, or impressive, or happy all the time. It's a life turned toward God, seeing God, and made more human by it, not less. A God glorified by people being small and miserable wasn't the God Irenaeus knew. And notice when he wrote it. Lyon had just lost its martyrs. Irenaeus didn't pretend life was easy. Yet he wrote that God's glory looks like a person coming fully alive.
screen: `AGAINST THE SECRET TEACHERS.` · `ONE GOD MADE IT ALL GOOD.` · `GLORIA DEI VIVENS HOMO.` · `LIFE IS SEEING GOD.` · then, large: `FULLY ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Feel your body for a moment: your feet, your hands, the air coming in, part of the good world, Irenaeus says, not a cage. Then pick one ordinary thing ahead of you today, a meal, a walk, a conversation, washing a pan, and picture doing it with all of you there, no scrolling, no half-listening. If you pray, offer that one thing to God before you begin.
Irenaeus. The bishop of Lyon who heard Polycarp as a boy and said the glory of God is a human being fully alive. Today's word.
Your line: fully alive. Not busier or more impressive, just more human. That's day seven hundred nine.

710.title: Perpetua and Felicity (203)
710.hook: a young noblewoman and her enslaved companion, whose own prison diary survives
710.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saints Perpetua and Felicity as a memorial in the Church's calendar, and both are named among the martyrs in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Irenaeus: the glory of God is a human being fully alive. Your line was fully alive.

The darkness scared her. She had never known a place like it. The heat of the crowd, the soldiers shoving, and worst of all, worry for her baby. A young mother wrote that, in a prison in North Africa. Her name was Vibia Perpetua: well born, educated, married, nursing an infant son. Arrested with her was Felicity, an enslaved woman, heavily pregnant. They were catechumens, still preparing for baptism. And because Perpetua kept a record, her own words survive.
screen: `THE DARKNESS SCARED HER.` → `A PRISON IN NORTH AFRICA.` → `A MOTHER AND A MOTHER-TO-BE.`

segments.voice: The text is called the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity. First, her own hand. The narrator says that from here on, Perpetua tells the story herself, as she left it written with her own hand. A prisoner's notes, from the inside. Second, the baby. Deacons pay the guards so the prisoners can move to a better part of the jail for a few hours, and Perpetua nurses her son. When she's allowed to keep him with her, she writes that the prison suddenly felt like a palace. Her father comes again and again, begging her to give in for his sake and the child's. She grieves for him, and she doesn't give in. Third, Felicity. Pregnant women weren't put to death, and she's afraid she'll be held back while her friends die without her. Her companions pray with her, and she goes into labor. A guard sneers: if you cry out like this now, what will you do in front of the beasts? She answers: now I'm the one who suffers. Then another will be in me, who will suffer for me, because I'll be suffering for him. She gives birth to a daughter, and a Christian woman raises the girl as her own. Fourth, the arena. The text says Perpetua, thrown down, gets up, sees Felicity on the ground, and lifts her to her feet. The two stand together. Before they die, they give each other the kiss of peace. A noblewoman and an enslaved woman. At Mass, the first Eucharistic Prayer still names them both.
screen: `IN HER OWN HAND.` · `A BABY IN THE PRISON.` · `FELICITY GIVES BIRTH.` · `SHE LIFTS HER TO HER FEET.` · then, large: `THE KISS OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a young mother you know, a friend, a sister, a neighbor, or someone you saw on the bus with a stroller and a tired face. Think of the night feeds, the worry, the not knowing, and hold her there a while. If you pray, ask God to give her rest and help; if you don't, simply wish her strength.

711.title: Origen and Alexandria
711.hook: a brilliant teacher who read scripture on many levels; some of his ideas were later rejected
711.howItsDone: Catholic teaching distinguishes the literal sense of scripture from its spiritual senses, and the practice of lectio divina reads a short passage slowly, more than once, letting it speak in layers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Perpetua and Felicity, and their passio. Your line was sisters in the arena.

A father in Alexandria makes his son learn a passage of scripture every day. The boy, Origen, isn't satisfied with the plain words. He keeps asking: but what does it mean, underneath? Eusebius says his father scolded him for asking questions beyond his years, and was secretly delighted. Then persecution comes, and the father is arrested. The boy wants to go and die with him, and his mother, out of options, hides all his clothes so he can't leave the house. He writes his father a letter instead.
screen: `A PASSAGE EVERY DAY.` → `WHAT DOES IT MEAN, UNDERNEATH?` → `HIS MOTHER HID HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Origen grew up to teach in Alexandria, in Egypt, and Eusebius says he was put in charge of instructing people preparing for baptism. He never stopped asking the boy's question. First, his picture. In On First Principles, Origen says scripture is like a human being, with a body, a soul and a spirit. The body is the plain sense: the story, what happened, what the words say. The soul is what the passage asks of the way you live. The spirit is what it shows about Christ and the life to come. Second, the Church kept the layers. The Catechism of the Catholic Church still speaks of the literal sense of scripture and the spiritual senses built on it, and insists the spiritual senses rest on the literal one. Its example: the crossing of the Red Sea is a real escape from Egypt, and it's also read as a sign of Christ's victory and of baptism. Third, the caution. Origen was a bold thinker, and some of his guesses were later judged to go too far. The Church rejected certain ideas linked with his name, like souls existing before their bodies. He isn't honored as a saint. Fourth, why it matters. A verse can be read once, closed and filed. Or it can be read again and again and give something new each time, the way a friend of many years can still surprise you. Origen read that way all his life, starting as a boy who wanted to know what was underneath.
screen: `BODY, SOUL AND SPIRIT.` · `THE LITERAL SENSE COMES FIRST.` · `SOME IDEAS WENT TOO FAR.` · `READ IT AGAIN.` · then, large: `LAYERS OF MEANING.`

segments.voice: Here's a line from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing." Read it plainly first: someone in charge, someone looked after, nobody going without, and the next verse sets the scene in a place of pasture and water. Then say it again slowly and let it ask about your own life: what do you want today that you might not need, and where are you being led? If you pray, say the line once more as a prayer.

712.title: Cyprian (d. 258)
712.hook: you can't have God for your father without the Church for your mother; and the fight over welcoming back the lapsed
712.howItsDone: Catholics remember Saint Cyprian together with Pope Saint Cornelius in the Church's calendar, and both are named in the Roman Canon; the sacrament of penance is the Church's ordinary way of welcoming back those who have fallen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Origen, who read scripture in layers: body, soul and spirit. Your line was layers of meaning.

The persecution is over, and the church in Carthage has a problem nobody prepared for. During it, an emperor's order told everyone to sacrifice to the gods. Some Christians refused, and suffered for it. Some ran. And some gave in: they burned the incense, or bought a certificate saying they had. Now the danger has passed, and those who gave in are standing at the church door, asking to come home. The bishop, Cyprian, has to answer them. So does everyone else.
screen: `THE PERSECUTION IS OVER.` → `SOME GAVE IN.` → `NOW THEY'RE AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, Cyprian's own position was awkward. When the persecution began, he went into hiding and led his people by letters. He said it was for their sake. Some said he'd run. So when he speaks about those who fell, he isn't speaking from a pedestal. The church called them the lapsed, the fallen. Second, two loud answers. Some of the confessors, Christians who had suffered and survived, wrote notes of peace welcoming the lapsed back at once, no questions asked. At Rome, a priest named Novatian took the opposite line: those who had denied Christ could never be taken back by the Church. Third, Cyprian's way: not at once, and not never. In his book On the Lapsed, he grieves over them. He asks for real repentance, time, and a decision by the bishops together, not a quick pardon from one person. And then, a welcome home. Fourth, the picture behind it all. In another book, On the Unity of the Church, he writes the line on today's screen, put simply: no one can have God for his Father who doesn't have the Church for his mother. A mother can be strict. A mother also keeps the door open and sets a place at the table. For Cyprian, that was the Church: one family, holding the line and holding out its arms. He died a martyr in the end. The account says that when the sentence was read, he answered: thanks be to God.
screen: `SOME GAVE IN.` · `AT ONCE, OR NEVER?` · `REPENTANCE, THEN HOME.` · `GOD FATHER, CHURCH MOTHER.` · then, large: `THE CHURCH IS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who drifted away, from your family, your friends, your parish, or from you, and hold their face a moment, honestly, the hurt included if there is some. Then ask what a first step back toward them would look like: not pretending nothing happened, just an open door. If you pray, hold them before God.

713.title: Lawrence the deacon (258)
713.hook: ordered to hand over the Church's treasures, he brings the poor
713.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Lawrence in the Church's calendar, and deacons today still proclaim the Gospel at Mass and are charged with service, especially to the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyprian, who called the lapsed home through repentance. Your line was the Church is mother.

Bring me the treasures of the Church. That's the demand put to a deacon in Rome named Lawrence. Tradition says the officials expected gold and silver. Lawrence doesn't argue, and he doesn't run. He promises to show them. The next day he arrives with a crowd behind him: the poor of the church, the people it fed and looked after. He points at them. These, he says, are the treasures of the Church.
screen: `BRING ME THE TREASURES.` → `HE PROMISES TO SHOW THEM.` → `HE BRINGS A CROWD.`

segments.voice: The story is told by Ambrose, a bishop writing in a later generation. First, what a deacon was for. In the Acts of the Apostles, the Christians in Jerusalem complain that their widows are being overlooked in the daily care. The apostles don't want to leave preaching to serve tables, so seven men are chosen to look after it. The church came to call that ministry the deacon's. In Justin's Sunday, the deacons carry the bread to those who are absent, and the collection goes to orphans, widows and strangers. Lawrence served in that line, in Rome. Second, his bishop. Ambrose says Lawrence watched his bishop, Sixtus, being led away to die, and cried out: where are you going, father, without your son? Sixtus told him he would follow soon. Third, the treasures. When the order comes to hand over the Church's wealth, Lawrence shows them the people. In the same book, Ambrose argues that the Church has gold to spend on those in need, not to store up, and adds that the poor truly were treasures, because Christ lives in them. Fourth, the gridiron. Tradition, which Ambrose repeats, says Lawrence was put to death by being roasted, and that he joked even then: this side's done, turn me over. Whatever the details, his name is still read in the Roman Canon at Mass. And the story keeps asking every parish the same question: when someone asks to see your treasure, who do you point at?
screen: `A DEACON SERVES TABLES.` · `WHERE ARE YOU GOING, FATHER?` · `HE SHOWS THEM THE PEOPLE.` · `THE GRIDIRON.` · then, large: `THESE ARE THE TREASURES.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who is poor, in money or in some other way: a man on the same corner, a family your parish helps, a lonely neighbor; use a name if you know one. Look at them the way Lawrence did, as what the Church would point at if someone asked to see its wealth, and notice what changes in you. If you pray, say their name to God.
Lawrence the deacon. The Roman deacon who, ordered to hand over the Church's treasures, brought the poor. Today's word.

714.title: Agnes (c. 304)
714.hook: a girl of about twelve who would not give up her faith; lambs are blessed on her feast
714.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Agnes in the Church's calendar; in Rome, lambs are blessed on her feast and their wool is used for the pallia given to metropolitan archbishops, and at every Mass the people say or sing the Lamb of God before communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lawrence the deacon, who showed the officials the poor. Your line was these are the treasures.

Lambs, carried into a church in Rome, and blessed. It happens on the feast of a saint named Agnes, at a church built over the place tradition says she was buried. Their wool is later spun and woven into a pallium, a narrow band the Pope gives to metropolitan archbishops to wear over their vestments. It's a gentle ceremony for a story that isn't gentle at all. Agnes was a girl, killed for refusing to give up her faith.
screen: `LAMBS IN A CHURCH IN ROME.` → `WOOL FOR THE PALLIUM.` → `A GIRL NAMED AGNES.`

segments.voice: One early witness is Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, in his book On Virgins. First, her age. Ambrose says she is said to have been martyred at twelve. He finds it hard to take in: a cruelty that didn't spare even so young an age, and a faith that wasn't stopped by it. Second, the chains. The officials brought out chains, Ambrose says, and they were too big; her hands were too small for them. Too young to be sentenced, he says, and yet ready to win. She stood, prayed, and bowed her head. Third, the name. Augustine, preaching on her feast, noticed it: Agnes in Latin sounds like agna, a lamb, and in Greek it means pure. Artists picture her with a lamb in her arms, and the lambs in Rome are blessed on her day. Fourth, why a lamb. At Mass, just before communion, Catholics sing or say the Agnus Dei, Lamb of God, taking up the words of John the Baptist in the Gospel of John: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world." A lamb is small, it doesn't fight back, and in that Gospel line it's the one who carries the world's sin. Agnes, small, refusing to fight and refusing to give in, became a picture of that Lamb. Her name is read among the martyrs in the Roman Canon, along with Perpetua and Felicity.
